title: Why a Defender made in Pune costs up to Rs 34 lakh less
subtitle: JLR has started building the Defender 110 in India, and a much smaller import tax on parts kits is behind the big price cut.
content_html:
Picture this. The same big Land Rover Defender that cost Rs 1.52 crore last week now costs Rs 1.18 crore. The engine is the same. The badge is the same. The only big change is the city where the car is put together. On Tuesday, 27 October 2026, JLR India said it has started making the Defender 110 in Pune, and cut prices by up to Rs 34 lakh for the top version.

So how can moving a factory line knock lakhs off a price tag? The answer is a tax, a box of parts and a team of workers in Pune.

What exactly happened in Pune?

JLR is the British car company behind Jaguar, Range Rover and Defender, and it is owned by Tata Motors. Until now, every Defender sold in India came fully built from abroad. The Defender is made at JLR's plant in Nitra, Slovakia, and that plant will keep making the global versions, ET reported.

Now one version, the Defender 110 in X-Dynamic HSE trim, will be built in Pune for Indian buyers. India is the first market outside Europe to make the Defender. The other Defenders, like the Defender 90, the Defender 130 and the OCTA, will still come in fully built.

Here are the new prices, all ex-showroom New Delhi, as listed by Rushlane:

  • 3.0 litre petrol: Rs 1.18 crore, down from Rs 1.52 crore (Rs 34 lakh less)
  • 3.0 litre diesel: Rs 1.18 crore, down from Rs 1.52 crore (Rs 34 lakh less)
  • 2.0 litre petrol: Rs 99 lakh, down from about Rs 1.13 crore (about Rs 14 lakh less)

That is a cut of about 22% on the bigger engines and about 12% on the smaller one. Deliveries of the Pune-made cars start on 15 November.

Why does making a car here make it cheaper?

Think of a samosa stall. If the stall buys ready samosas from a far away shop, it pays the shop's price plus a big delivery charge. If it buys the flour, potatoes and spices and fries the samosas itself, the delivery charge on raw things is much smaller. The samosa costs less to sell.

Cars work in a similar way. When a car comes into India fully built, the trade calls it a CBU, short for completely built unit. India puts a heavy import tax, called customs duty, on these cars. According to ClearTax's guide to car import duty, a fully built car can face a total duty of about 110% to 115% of its value, once the basic duty and an extra farm cess are added.

The other way is a CKD kit, short for completely knocked down. The car comes in pieces: body panels, engine, seats, wires, all packed in boxes. Workers in India put the pieces together. The same ClearTax guide says these kits pay a much lower duty, about 10% to 20% depending on how much is already joined.

The Pune Defender uses exactly this kit route, Rushlane reported. Less tax at the port means the company can charge less in the showroom.

Why would JLR want to give up all that money?

A lower price is not charity. JLR wants to sell more cars. The company expects sales volumes to rise by up to 20% after this move. It sold 9,000 Defenders in India in the last three and a half years. The Defender is its best seller here.

JLR has also tried this before. After it began building the Range Rover and Range Rover Sport in India, the brand saw sales grow about 2.5 times, Autocar India reported. The Defender now joins locally built versions of the Range Rover, Range Rover Sport, Velar, Evoque and Discovery Sport.

There is a race too. In FY26, JLR India sold 6,031 vehicles and was the third biggest luxury carmaker, ET reported. Mercedes-Benz India sold 19,363 and BMW India sold 17,301. JLR's India head, Rajan Amba, told ET: "We are a strong number 3." He also said there is still a long way to go to close the gap with number two.

What does this mean for Pune and its workers?

When a car is built from a kit, the work of putting it together happens in India instead of in Europe. That means more work for the plant in Pune. JLR has room for it: the company has an installed capacity to make 12,000 vehicles a year in India, Amba told ET. That is about double the 6,031 it sold last year, so the factory can grow.

The reports do not give a number for new hires. But the idea is simple. If more Defenders roll out of Pune, more hands are needed on that line.

Buyers also get more for their money. The 3.0 litre versions now come with extra features, worth up to Rs 17 lakh, as standard, and the 2.0 litre version gets features worth up to Rs 6.5 lakh, Rushlane reported.

Why did buyers wait, and why might they stop waiting?

Luxury car buyers in India have been holding back. Amba told ET that talk of price cuts under trade deals has made some customers delay buying, because they hope prices will fall later. It is like waiting for a Diwali sale before buying a phone.

A clear price cut of up to Rs 34 lakh gives those buyers a reason to stop waiting. Amba also expects India's luxury car market to grow at least 15% this calendar year.

For anyone watching Indian business, the bigger lesson is about "Make in India". When import taxes on finished goods are high, companies that build here can sell for much less. That is why JLR now builds versions of six of its models in India. Here is an older ET Now video on JLR's Pune plant:

The quick recap

  • On 27 October 2026, JLR India began making the Defender 110 in Pune.
  • The top versions now cost Rs 1.18 crore, Rs 34 lakh less than before.
  • The cut comes mostly from paying lower import duty on parts kits instead of fully built cars.
  • JLR expects up to 20% more sales and has room to make 12,000 vehicles a year in India.
  • Deliveries of Pune-made Defenders begin on 15 November.
